results.summary: SPELL is a hardware implementation of a minimal stack-based programming language created for The Skull CTF. It executes a cryptic program stored in EEPROM, using a stack machine architecture with a shift register for serial output. The design is intended as a security challenge, requiring external hardware to load and run the program. No silicon test report is provided, so its hardware behavior is not confirmed.

This project implements a VGA display controller with a clock generator, timer, and RTC functionality. It uses a PMOD interface for external connections and is designed for educational purposes. The design is implemented in Verilog and targets the Tiny Tapeout platform. No silicon test report is provided, so its hardware behavior is not confirmed.

This project implements a VGA graphics controller with a machine-learning accelerator. It uses a PMOD interface for external connections and is designed for educational purposes. The design is implemented in Verilog and targets the Tiny Tapeout platform. No silicon test report is provided, so its hardware behavior is not confirmed.

This is a simple Snake game with VGA output, controlled by four directional buttons. The game uses a finite state machine and counters to manage game logic and display. It requires external VGA monitor and buttons for interaction. No silicon test report is provided, so its hardware behavior is not confirmed.

This is a Pong game with VGA output, controlled by two players. The game uses a finite state machine and counters to manage game logic and display. It requires external VGA monitor and buttons for interaction. No silicon test report is provided, so its hardware behavior is not confirmed.

This circuit outputs the string 'tiny tapeout' to a 7-segment display. It uses a shift register and a clock generator to sequence the characters. The design is implemented in Wokwi and is intended as a learning exercise. No silicon test report is provided, so its hardware behavior is not confirmed.

This circuit is a game that uses a single input switch to control gameplay. The input is debounced and edge-triggered, with rising and falling edges converted to pulses. The game is designed to work better with a switch rather than a button. No silicon test report is provided, so its hardware behavior is not confirmed.

This circuit uses a circular buffer of D flip-flops as a selector and D flip-flops for memory, with combinational logic for the display. It is implemented in Wokwi and is intended for educational purposes. The design demonstrates sequential logic and memory elements. No silicon test report is provided, so its hardware behavior is not confirmed.

This is a basic first test design that uses a pair of inverters and a pair of AND gates to detect a secret code on three input pins. It requires no external hardware and is intended as a learning exercise for the Tiny Tapeout process. The design is implemented in Wokwi and is a simple combinational logic circuit. No silicon test report is provided, so its hardware behavior is not confirmed.

This circuit acts as a configurable timer that counts down from a value set on its inputs (0 to 7) and displays the remaining time in binary form on LEDs. It uses a counter and a clock generator to manage the countdown. The design is implemented in Wokwi and is intended for educational purposes. No silicon test report is provided, so its hardware behavior is not confirmed.
